---
title: "Preface"
---

## Why this book exists

There are good books on online experimentation and good books on causal
inference — but they sit on opposite sides of a gap. The experimentation
literature (Kohavi, Tang & Xu) is platform-centric but light on modern causal
ML. The causal-inference literature (Facure, Cunningham, Chernozhukov et al.)
is method-rich but not built around *running experiments on a platform*:
switchback, CUPED/CUPAC, always-valid inference, metric governance, marketplace
interference.

This book is the bridge: **causal inference as practiced inside a modern
experimentation platform.** It is organized by the *problem you face when
running experiments*, not by method family — so each chapter opens with the
platform problem and then reaches for whatever method solves it, whether that
method comes from the A/B-testing tradition, the econometrics tradition, or the
causal-ML tradition.

## Two conventions, every chapter

1. **The platform problem.** Each chapter starts by naming the concrete
   experimentation problem it addresses. Methods are tools, not the subject.

2. **Validate against ground truth.** Each chapter ends by recovering a *known*
   effect from a simulated data-generating process (Vega), reporting bias and
   coverage. This is the pedagogical move no real-data textbook can make: you
   see the estimator hit a number we set on purpose. It is also, not by
   coincidence, the test suite for the companion platform.

## The companion platform

The methods here are implemented in **Lyra** (an experimentation platform:
assignment, event log, governed metrics, guardrails, a causal inference engine,
a scorecard) and validated by **Vega** (the data-generating + simulation +
Monte-Carlo harness layer). The book and the platform share a spine; Part XIV
and Appendix A are, in effect, Lyra/Vega's documentation.

## How to read it

- **Practitioners** can read any Part standalone; the "platform problem" opener
  makes each one self-contained.
- **Learners** should read Parts I–IV in order — that is the minimum viable,
  correctly-done experiment readout — then branch by interest.
- All code is runnable. Python by default; R chapters declare `engine: knitr`.

## Status

This is a living document, written in lockstep with the platform. Chapters ship
when their methods are built and validated, not before.
